title: Helix AI - migration & eval parity discovery
summary: Discovery call for migrating Helix AI from a hybrid setup (OpenAI hosted + on-prem vLLM for low latency) to Redwood. Main concerns: model eval parity vs OpenAI/Anthropic, compatibility for custom tokenizers and TGI/vLLM pipelines, p99 latency at scale, cost tradeoffs, and security (SAML, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next steps: Redwood to send security pack, propose pilot benchmark config, Helix to share sample prompt set and traffic profile, schedule dedicated benchmark run next week.
action_items: Maya Chen: send security & compliance packet and SOC2 report by 2025-07-10
Rafael Ortiz: propose benchmark config (model variants, batch sizes, kernel configs) by 2025-07-14
Leah Kim: share sample prompt set, token distributions, and current vLLM config by 2025-07-11
Noah Rivera: provide network/VPC constraints and list of required audit logs by 2025-07-12
next_steps: Redwood to run a small pilot with Helix's prompts on Dedicated or Private (TBD)
Schedule 60-min benchmark session w/ SE pair next Wed (2025-07-16)
Exchange security docs and outline of SSO/KMS integration plan
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09 14:30 PT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aaron Patel (Helix CTO), Leah Kim (Helix ML Eng), Noah Rivera (Helix Infra), Sofia Park (Product)

00:00 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and joining me is Rafael, one of our SEs. We wanted to kick off with a quick agenda — understand your current stack and constraints, dig into model compatibility/eval parity questions, and talk pilot scope. Does that sound right?
00:12 - Aaron Patel: Yep that's perfect. We'll start with context; thanks.
00:20 - Leah Kim: Quick note, audio is fine. We have about an hour.
00:25 - Rafael Ortiz: Great. Can you give us a quick overview of what Helix is running today and where the pain points are?
00:33 - Aaron Patel: Sure. So currently we run a hybrid: for public-facing features we call OpenAI for most generation, mostly for convenience and quality. For latency-sensitive internal features — scoring and real-time assistants — we run vLLM on a k8s cluster in our colo. The problems are twofold: cost unpredictability and operating burden of the vLLM stack — kernel/build issues, occasional OOMs when sequences spike — and we see some gaps in eval parity between hosted OpenAI responses and our on-prem runs. That's the high level.
01:05 - Maya Chen: Helpful. When you say eval parity, do you mean qualitative differences in hallucination rates or prompt-behavior mismatches?
01:12 - Leah Kim: Both. For a subset of prompts, the OpenAI responses are slightly different — tone and fact accuracy — and our teams worry that switching to a different hosted endpoint will change product UX. We need high fidelity to the current model's outputs for end-user consistency.
01:25 - Rafael Ortiz: Understood. Two quick clarifying qs: which models are you calling on OpenAI (or Anthropic) today, and what does your vLLM stack use — is it running exact same weights, or distilled/quantized variants?
01:35 - Aaron Patel: We're primarily on GPT-4o via API for some flows and Claude-2 for a few experiments; on-prem is a trimmed-down Llama2-derived 70B that we quantize to 4-bit for cost. We also have a TGI-based pipeline in one team; it's been a mixed bag.
01:52 - Rafael Ortiz: Okay. So compatibility will hinge on model weights and tokenizer differences, plus runtime kernels. With Redwood we support a bunch of open models and can host custom weights. We also do kernel selection for quantized paths and optimize KV cache handling. But parity testing is important.
02:10 - Sofia Park: Quick question — can Redwood run the exact same quantized weights we have? Our legal/compliance folks are picky about model provenance.
02:18 - Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we can ingest customer-provided weights in Dedicated and Private modes; we'd run them through our onboarding checks. For Hosted we have curated models; for your use-case Dedicated or Private looks more likely since you want control over weights and auditability.
02:32 - Noah Rivera: Network question: our infra team needs to know if Redwood Private can run inside our VPC with strict egress rules and KMS/HSM for keys.
02:42 - Maya Chen: Absolutely — Private supports a customer-controlled control plane and can be deployed in VPC or on-prem. KMS integrations and HSMs are supported; we'll include the exact network diagrams in the security pack.
02:54 - Aaron Patel: Cost is also a driver. If we go Hosted, our token cost with OpenAI is predictable but sometimes spikes. What's Redwood's cost delta on a per-token basis and how does Dedicated pricing compare when you factor reserved capacity?
03:07 - Maya Chen: High level: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is a commit model with lower unit costs for steady traffic and offers predictability. We can run a quick pricing sketch after we see your traffic profile. Rafael, do you want to add about batching/caching options?
03:20 - Rafael Ortiz: Yeah — performance and unit cost are often tradeoffs. We automatically suggest batching, KV prefix caching for repeated prompts, and quantization profiles. For real-time flows, we tune for low batch sizes and use fast kernels; for high-throughput background batches we push larger batch sizes. We can aim for p95/p99 targets in the pilot.
03:40 - Leah Kim: Important: we need p99 under 200ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) for our assistant use-case. Is that realistic?
03:47 - Rafael Ortiz: On Dedicated with optimized kernels and small batch sizes, yes that's achievable for many models. If you're using 70B quantized 4-bit, p99 may be higher — depends on hardware. We'll propose GPU types and kernel settings. For strict sub-200ms p99 you may need a mix: smaller model variants or specialized low-latency hardware.
04:06 - Aaron Patel: About eval parity — if we run your runtime with our quantized weights, can we reproduce OpenAI GPT-4o outputs?
04:13 - Rafael Ortiz: Reproducing GPT-4o exactly isn't possible unless you have the same proprietary weights. But you can test behavioral parity: we'll run your prompts against your current OpenAI calls, capture outputs, and compare to outputs from the model you host on Redwood. Differences often come from model family, temperature, tokenization and decoding parameters. We have a small eval harness to compute similarity metrics (BLEU-ish, embedding cosine, and semantic evals) as well as human spot checks.
04:40 - Sofia Park: Do you support the same tokenizer APIs? Our pipelines use custom tokenizers and special BOS/EOS tokens.
04:47 - Rafael Ortiz: We support custom tokenizers in Dedicated/Private. We also can map token offsets and ensure prefix caching works with your tokenizer. There are occasional edge cases with TGI compatibility; we sometimes see small tokenization id shifts — we'll validate during onboarding.
05:05 - Leah Kim: We also use function-calling and some structured outputs. Any compatibility caveats?
05:12 - Rafael Ortiz: We support function/tool calling and structured output. Hosted supports standard patterns; Dedicated gives you more control over determinism. We'll test your exact tool schema.
05:21 - Aaron Patel: Security check: SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit log retention — can you meet enterprise requirements?
05:30 - Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood has SOC2 Type II; we offer SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC, and configurable audit log retention. We'll attach the SOC2 report and our security questionnaire in the pack.
05:42 - Noah Rivera: From infra perspective, during pilot we need to see logs, traces, and per-token latency breakdowns to correlate with our service traces.
05:51 - Rafael Ortiz: The Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. We can stream logs into your SIEM if needed.
06:02 - Aaron Patel: Timeline: we want a pilot by end of month — two weeks to validate parity and perf. Is that feasible?
06:09 - Maya Chen: Feasible. We'll propose a 2-week pilot: week 1 — setup + baseline runs; week 2 — tuned benchmarking and result review. Rafael will propose the exact config.
06:18 - Rafael Ortiz: I'll include model variants, batch sizes, hardware tiers (A100 vs H100 vs RTX-class), and quantization paths. Also a fallback policy: canary rollouts and A/B test configs so you can route percentage of production traffic.
06:34 - Leah Kim: One more: our legal wants to confirm data retention rules for Hosted — we can't send PII to third-party hosted endpoints. So Private or Dedicated is likely.
06:43 - Maya Chen: Understood — we'll outline retention, encryption, and the Private option which keeps data within your VPC.
06:50 - Aaron Patel: Great. Thanks. Any final questions?
06:55 - Sofia Park: No. Please send the security docs and the pilot runbook.
07:00 - Maya Chen: We'll send the pack and propose times for the benchmark session. Rafael, anything else?
07:05 - Rafael Ortiz: I'll also ask for sample prompts and traffic shape so we can size the reserved capacity.
07:10 - Aaron Patel: We'll share those by Friday.
07:15 - Maya Chen: Terrific — recap of next steps in chat. Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript — auto-generated segments may have small transcription errors: e.g., 'v-L-M' vs 'vLLM', 'T G I' vs 'TGI'.]
